strengths: Novel dataset (WHOOPS-AHA!) specifically designed for mechanistic analysis of multimodal knowledge conflicts, filling a gap in VLM interpretability research

Rigorous experimental methodology with multiple validation approaches: logit lens analysis, targeted causal interventions, control experiments on random heads, and ablation studies with consistent results across two model architectures

Clear and interpretable findings about functional dissociation between components: attention blocks favor visual context (61% attention to image) while MLP blocks support factual knowledge, localized to ~20 heads in final layers

Demonstrates that attention-based attribution achieves superior precision in identifying critical image regions compared to gradient-based methods, with sharp improvement from ablating top 10-30% of patches

Well-designed interventions constrained within plausible ranges (λ ∈ [-3,3]) with KL-divergence analysis showing quality degradation, and effective control experiment showing specificity to identified heads
Comprehensive presentation with clear visualizations, documented prompts for reproducibility, and honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Logit lens limitations inadequately addressed: relying on single representative factual/counterfactual token per example oversimplifies the generative landscape and may miss important aspects of conflict resolution across full generations

Limited dataset scope and generalizability: ~430 examples from synthetic WHOOPS! images after filtering; unclear transfer to real-world conflicts (outdated knowledge, natural ambiguities); only commonsense knowledge conflicts studied; inter-annotator agreement for manual verification not reported

Arbitrary methodological choices lacking justification: selection of 20 heads is post-hoc (only ~5% improvement beyond this point); threshold parameter τ is ad-hoc without sensitivity analysis; intervention range λ ∈ [-3,3] motivated by KL divergence but somewhat artificial; no statistical significance testing

Limited mechanistic insight: identifies which heads matter but provides minimal understanding of why they develop this functionality or what representations they encode; interventions demonstrate causality without explaining underlying mechanisms

Intervention method constrained to final token position attention only; ignores possible contributions from MLP blocks, visual encoders, or intermediate layers; quality degradation at higher magnitudes (|λ| > 3) severely limits practical applicability

Attribution method comparison narrow: only compares to gradients without other attribution techniques; no human evaluation of identified regions beyond visual inspection of two examples; uses same threshold τ for both methods potentially biasing comparison

Scope limitations reduce generalizability: only 2 models tested; focuses on text generation without evaluating on other VLM tasks (VQA, image-text matching); unclear transfer to other conflict types or domains; concurrent work (Golovanevsky et al. 2025a) addresses similar questions

Limited practical impact: paper is mostly diagnostic without actionable solutions for mitigating hallucinations; no experiments showing whether identified heads could be pruned to improve robustness; relies on synthetic data that may not reflect real hallucination scenarios

strengths: Novel research direction addressing underexplored gap: first dataset explicitly designed for mechanistic analysis of multimodal knowledge conflicts in VLMs
Well-constructed WHOOPS-AHA! dataset with careful controls: clear factual/counterfactual distinction, GPT-4o generation with manual verification, addresses specific research question
Rigorous, multi-faceted methodology: logit lens analysis + targeted interventions + ablation studies + control experiments (random heads), providing strong triangulation for causal claims

Clear mechanistic insights with interpretable findings: functional separation between attention (favors visual) and MLP (favors knowledge), localization to final layers, distinct attention patterns (61% vs 29% to image), strong causal evidence (22%→74% accuracy shift)
Consistent cross-model validation: findings replicate across LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b with similar patterns
Advances attribution methods: demonstrates attention-based attribution outperforms gradient-based methods for identifying conflict-driving regions with superior precision
Excellent clarity and presentation: well-organized paper with effective figures, clear examples, and precise writing
Reproducibility: planned code/data release, clear methodology, reasonable computational requirements (15 GPU hours), use of public implementations
weaknesses: Limited model coverage: only 2 models tested (both 7B-12B scale), unclear generalization to larger models or different architectures (GPT-4V, Claude, etc.)

Dataset limitations significantly constrain scope: synthetic/curated data from single source, only 436-432 examples, single-token completions (doesn't capture full generative behavior), limited to one conflict type (visual anomalies vs commonsense)

Foundational technique concerns: Logit Lens has known distortions (acknowledged by authors), yet it's used to identify the very heads being intervened on, potentially affecting identification reliability

Narrow intervention scope: focus only on attention heads at final token position limits understanding; doesn't capture MLP or visual encoder contributions; modification of only final attention row may miss other mechanisms
Limited practical impact: acknowledged as diagnostic/exploratory work, intervention approach not ready-to-deploy; findings provide understanding but not actionable solutions

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: unclear why factual/counterfactual heads emerge (architectural necessity vs training artifact), how mechanisms develop during training, or why gradient attribution saturates earlier
Concurrent related work reduces novelty: Golovanevsky et al. (2025a) addresses similar questions with steering vectors; while approaches differ, timing raises novelty concerns
Attribution comparison limitations: only compares attention vs gradient methods; doesn't evaluate other attribution approaches; lacks mechanistic explanation for attention's superiority
Statistical rigor gaps: limited error bars/confidence intervals, no significance testing, single-token focus limits statistical power
Generalization questions unaddressed: unclear how findings transfer to text-only conflicts, longer sequences, or other semantic conflict types beyond visual anomalies

strengths: Well-motivated research question addressing an important gap: understanding how VLMs resolve conflicts between internal knowledge and visual evidence

Carefully designed WHOOPS-AHA! dataset with explicit requirements (controlled induction, token-level precision, commonsense grounding, topical generality) and thorough validation combining LLM-as-judge and human evaluation

Rigorous mechanistic analysis with multiple complementary tools (Logit Lens, targeted intervention, gradient-based attribution) and strong causal evidence from interventions with appropriate controls (random heads, POPE benchmark)

Clear mechanistic insights with substantial effect sizes: functional separation between attention blocks (favor visual) and MLPs (favor factual), concentrated in upper layers with only ~20 heads mediating conflict

Novel finding that attention-based attribution outperforms gradient-based methods for visual localization, validated quantitatively on segmented images (median ratio 4.41 for Gemma3 vs 1.74 for gradients, p<0.01)
Generalization evidence beyond WHOOPS-AHA! showing 13-14/20 identical heads across Visual CounterFact dataset, suggesting transferable mechanisms
Excellent reproducibility documentation with comprehensive appendices, detailed prompts, hyperparameter justifications, and code availability
weaknesses: Severely limited architectural scope: only late-fusion models tested (LLaVA-NeXT, Gemma3); acknowledged but not addressed. Early/mid-fusion architectures may operate via fundamentally different mechanisms, limiting generalizability claims

Over-reliance on Logit Lens with known approximation errors (Belrose et al., 2023): projecting from non-final residual states introduces distortions, and interpreting as exact predictions is approximate. No validation that logit lens accurately reflects actual model behavior on this task

Oversimplified single-token completion setting: real VLMs generate free-form text with interdependent predictions. Selecting highest-probability tfact/tcofa tokens and focusing on final-position interventions may not scale to longer sequences or free-form generation

Dataset size and scope limitations: only ~436-432 examples after filtering (from ~500 images); post-hoc ambiguity filtering could introduce selection bias with fraction and impact not clearly reported. WHOOPS! images are synthetic; only commonsense conflicts studied; generalization to other conflict types unclear

Arbitrary methodological choices with limited justification: selecting exactly 20 heads justified post-hoc in Figure 10; intervention range λ ∈ [-3, 3] chosen for qualitative 'plausibility' rather than principled criteria; multiplicative intervention parameterization not compared with alternatives
Attribution evaluation limited to 20 images with SAM-3 segmentation validation not provided. Average Ratio metric is simple; no analysis of when gradients outperform attention-based attribution

Incomplete failure case analysis: limited discussion of when mechanisms break down or when gradient-based attribution is preferable. POPE validation only tests object presence, not general visual reasoning comprehensiveness

Gaps in distinguishing from concurrent work: differentiation from Golovanevsky et al. (2025a,b) and Hua et al. (2025) could be clearer; claimed distinction of 'implicit vs. explicit conflicts' may be superficial
